body_markdown:
We’ve officially made it through the summer. As the northern states wrap up driving season before it gets too cold and the southern parts of the country roll into more hospitable driving weather, we’ve updated all the pricing on[Hagerty Valuation Tools](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools) , and it’s time to examine the state of the market. In the weeks following a record-obliterating[Monterey Car Week](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/2026-monterey-car-week-auctions-shatter-record-with-756m-in-sales/) back in August, the market for enthusiast cars remains as divided as ever. Supercars, mainly modern Ferraris, still carry the headlines, while established and more attainable enthusiast cars have begun to tread water or deflate in value.


This split market isn’t new, but it is getting more defined as the year continues. While the increases in this latest update (which went live on October 1) were mainly concentrated in exotics, a few more affordable cars snuck in. Here are a few of the most noteworthy gainers from the past quarter (as calculated across all conditions).


*Have questions about how we arrived at these changes? You can read more about the methodology behind the Hagerty Price Guide[here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/how-the-hagerty-price-guide-is-made/) .*


## [2010–12 Porsche 911 GT3](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/2010/2010-porsche-911-gt3?id=aCn1I000000DGZkSAO)


Broad Arrow


**Average increase:** +64%


The 997.2 version of the 911 GT3, built from 2010 to 2012, represented the purest distillation of what Porsche’s engineers could extract from the rear-engined sports car formula. Powered by a naturally aspirated 3.8-liter flat-six engine producing 435 horsepower and an 8400-rpm redline, this generation of GT3 has built a reputation for mechanical purity that its turbocharged competitors couldn’t replicate. Essentially a major update of the 997.1, it brought revised suspension geometry, better downforce, and overall mechanical refinements to the model.


What set the 997.2 GT3 apart from its contemporaries wasn’t raw horsepower but rather the quality of driving experience and precision it offered to a skilled driver. The six-speed manual gearbox received wide praise as one of the finest in the world, while the naturally aspirated engine’s linear power delivery rewarded those willing to use the entire rev range. A Clubsport package added a roll cage, fire extinguisher, and harness bar for those who intended to use the car more seriously on track, and an RS variant offered an even more extreme, lightweight interpretation of the GT3 formula. Production ended in 2012 ahead of the transition to the 991 platform, and the 997.2 GT3 has since settled firmly into the collective memory of driving enthusiasts as one of the last truly analog, undiluted sports cars of its era.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Even to the casual Porschephile, 911 GT3s are serious, aspirational cars. They’re a real weapon on the track, even though many have never been within miles of a real paddock. Enthusiast excitement for these cars has always been there, but over the summer, it soared. From cars offered to insurance quotes, the direction is clear, with the numbers all trending upward.


Unfortunately, for the average enthusiast, the recent increase put these cars from out of reach to out of our league. A GT3 with significant mileage currently runs around $300,000, and if you want the RS model, that number doubles.


## [1990–2001 Lamborghini Diablo](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=lamborghini+diablo)


Broad Arrow


**Average increase:** +40%


Introduced in 1990, the Lamborghini Diablo replaced the[Countach](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=lamborghini+countach) as the raging bull’s flagship model. Initially designed by Marcello Gandini, the same mind behind the Countach and Miura, the Diablo’s lines were later heavily massaged by Chrysler, which owned Lamborghini at the time. It debuted with a powerful 5.7-liter V-12 engine producing around 485 hp—plenty of kick to push it past 200 mph, making it one of the fastest production cars then available.


The dramatic wedge shape and scissor doors carried on the Lamborghini tradition of being as wild to look at as it was to drive, all while feeling more refined and modern than its predecessor. Early models were rear-wheel drive only, but the 1993 introduction of the VT (Viscous Traction) variant brought all-wheel drive to the lineup, broadening its appeal without dulling its edge.


Lamborghini


Lamborghini/Massimiliano Serra


Lamborghini


Lamborghini


Over its 11-year production run, the Diablo evolved considerably through a series of updates and special editions. Audi’s acquisition of Lamborghini in 1998 brought improved build quality and engineering, resulting in the refined 6.0-liter SE and VT 6.0 models introduced in 2000, which took output to around 550 hp. Along the way, open-top Roadster versions, track-focused GT and GTRs, and stripped-out SVs (Sport Veloces) kept the range exciting. When production ended in 2001 with roughly 2900 units built, the Diablo passed the torch to the Murciélago, leaving behind a legacy as the last Lambo of the pre-Audi era, and as one of the most extreme, visually arresting supercars of its era.


It was only a matter of time before the Diablo got swept up in this year’s supercar craze, and the time has come. While all late-model V-12 Lambos fared well this past quarter, the Diablo is the one that took us by surprise. The 40% average increase for the VT model only tells part of the story, though, as it’s merely the midpoint for the Diablo’s broader increase.


The more desirable and rare GT models saw values climb by 60% on average, as did VT Roadsters. Meanwhile, the standard models from the early ’90s “only” increased by 17% on average. Diablos were never cheap cars, and the change reaffirms that the only Diablo most of us will afford is the one on a poster. A Diablo VT coupe in driver-quality (#3) condition is a $300,000 car or higher, while the ultra-rare GT is well into seven-figure territory after a strong showing at the Monterey sales. The big takeaway here is that the supercar craze is not slowing down yet: It’s spreading.


## [1999–2002 Mercedes-Benz CLK430](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mercedes~benz/clk430/2000/2000-mercedes~benz-clk430-base?id=aCn1I000000CxmySAC)


Hagerty Marketplace


**Average increase:** +26%


Built on the W208 chassis, the CLK430 occupied a sweet spot in the Mercedes-Benz lineup as an understated but elegant grand tourer that prioritized effortless performance and luxury over outright power and driver engagement. Under the gracefully curved hood sat the M113 4.3-liter V-8 engine producing 275 hp and paired with a five-speed automatic, delivering its thrust in the smooth manner that V-8 Mercedes of the era were known for. The styling was widely admired at the time, drawing on the larger E-Class for its proportions scaled down to C-Class sizing, giving it a presence well above its price point.


Inside, the CLK430 delivered the kind of cabin experience that Mercedes excelled at during this period, making it a genuinely nice place to sit. Wood trim, supportive leather seats, and a logically arranged dashboard created an environment that reinforced the car’s identity as a continent-crossing grand tourer. In a nominal sense, the CLK430 also served as the mass-production tie-in for the fearsome[CLK GTR](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mercedes~benz/clk_gtr/1998/1998-mercedes~benz-clk_gtr-base?id=aCn1I000000DS2MSAW) racing program, though the two cars shared little beyond a badge.


Mecum


Late ’90s through 2000s Mercedes have seen a surge in popularity across the board lately. Other models from the era that performed well this past quarter include the R230 (2003–12 SL) and the W204 (2008–15 C-Class). But even with recent growth, the CLK430 remains an attainable cruiser, with the best ones on the market running in the mid-$20,000 range. Beyond reputation, these cars have finally reached that age where the good ones are no longer viewed as a used Mercedes and are looked at through a more nostalgic and collector-focused lens.


## [1950–60 Saab 92 and 93](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=saab+93)


Bilweb Auctions


**Average increase:** +22%


For 1950, the Saab 92 was a remarkably forward-thinking automobile that established the Swedish brand’s reputation for unconventional engineering and aerodynamic innovation, despite having no prior experience building cars. Developed by a team of aircraft engineers, the 92 design had an unmistakable connection to aviation design, featuring a teardrop-shaped, fully integrated body with a drag coefficient of just 0.30, on par with cars produced today. Power came from a modest 764-cc two-stroke engine producing 25 hp, mounted transversely and driving the front wheels. The 92 was built to survive Scandinavian winters, and its robust, practical character combined with early rallying success quickly earned it a loyal following in Sweden and beyond.


Saab


[Ronnie Schreiber](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rschreiber/)


The Saab 93, which arrived in 1956 as a natural evolution of the 92, brought meaningful refinements while preserving the core philosophy of its predecessor. The most significant change was the adoption of a new 748-cc three-cylinder engine (still two-stroke), which smoothed out the roughness of the earlier twin and pushed output to around 33 hp. The body was subtly restyled with a wider rear window and a more contemporary appearance, and the interior saw improvements in comfort and ergonomics. The 93 also continued Saab’s early motorsports story, with rally drivers finding the car’s tenacious front-wheel-drive traction particularly well-suited to loose and slippery surfaces. Together, the 92 and 93 laid the ideological and engineering foundation for everything Saab would become—quirky, safety-conscious, and stubbornly independent in its thinking.


Saab 92 and 93 models are rare sights on the market, but they are an important part of the quirky, affordable end of the hobby. Even after a 22% average gain this quarter, a driver-quality 92 can be had for around $11,600, while the more refined 93 runs slightly higher at about $13,200. They aren’t cars for everyone. The two-stroke engine demands a different operating style and a steady diet of premix fuel to keep it running. But if you take the plunge, the sheer oddity will make you the center of attention at every stop.


## [1994–99 Ferrari F355](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=ferrari+f355)


Ferrari


**Average increase:** +19%


Unveiled at the 1994 Geneva Motor Show, the Ferrari F355 represented a significant leap forward from its predecessor, the[348](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=ferrari+348) . Powered by a five-valve 3.5-liter V-8 engine producing 375 hp, the F355 revved freely to 8500 rpm and delivered a soundtrack that became the stuff of legends among enthusiasts. Chief engineer Amedeo Felisa oversaw a thorough engineering overhaul that included a flat underbody with a diffuser (a concept borrowed from Ferrari’s Formula 1 program) and a dramatically improved suspension setup. The result was a car that felt genuinely alive and communicative, earning immediate praise from journalists and consumers alike for its balance, agility, and sheer mechanical artistry.


Broad Arrow


ISSIMI


Robb Williamson


Getty Images


The F355 was offered in three body styles: Berlinetta coupe, GTS with removable targa roof panel, and fully open-top Spider. Early cars exclusively got a six-speed manual, but Ferrari also offered its F1-style paddle-shift transmission from 1997 onward. Production ran from 1994 to 1999, during which around 11,000 examples sold, a high number by Ferrari standards of the era. When it was replaced by the[360 Modena](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/360/2000/2000-ferrari-360-modena?id=aCn1I000000DWB6SAO) , many felt the F355 had set a benchmark for driver engagement and emotional connection that would be difficult to surpass, and that reputation has only grown stronger in the years since, leading to a resurgence in popularity.


Since January, the market chatter in 2026 has been filled with Prancing Horse excitement. Well, Ferrari leads the way again. Frankly, this article could’ve been one big list of modern Ferraris, but the F355 was the standout increase over the summer. A ton of them appeared on the market, and all performed well. From average high-mileage cars to ultra-low-mileage ones in rarer colors, they all found enthusiastic buyers.


It wasn’t that long ago that the F355 represented one of the last great Ferraris you could snatch up under six figures. This is no longer the case. A driver-quality F355 coupe can cost over $200,000 now. Whether we’re talking F355s or anything else wearing Scuderia shields, the Ferrari boom didn’t lose steam over the summer and appears likely to continue apace through the end of the year.
